output.title: When a retainer quietly becomes a blank cheque
output.body:
The quiet cost of an open-ended retainer is not just the monthly fee. It is the way undefined work keeps expanding until nobody is sure what was actually being bought.

If you run a 1–10 person business, the real question is simpler: which one recurring workflow is dragging on your week? Repetitive customer questions, manual invoice work, or neglected leads are the usual suspects. In the representative scenario we use at Bareni, that can mean 8–10 hours a week of repeated work. That is a persona scenario, not a market statistic or an observed customer result.

The bounded alternative is a free 30-minute diagnostic. We look at one recurring workflow, say honestly whether AI fits, and if it does, define a fixed-price pilot with clear scope, measures, and intended timing. The timings are intended scopes, not guarantees. The point is to compare one defined pilot with an open-ended retainer before you keep paying for something that changes shape every month. A retainer can be useful; it should not be the default by accident.

That also keeps control where it belongs. Database, automation-tool, and API accounts stay in the customer’s name from the start, as policy and no-lock-in positioning. Retainer support is optional. For money movement and other high-risk decisions, human approval stays mandatory. No machine gets to sign the cheques; that would be a poor office policy.

We currently decline high-sensitivity medical, legal, and financial work, plus bulk cold-email automation and scan-heavy OCR-dependent workflows. If the workflow needs those, say so plainly and stop there.

A practical next step: write down one recurring workflow, its current weekly cost in hours or repeated vendor payments, and one concrete outcome that would justify a pilot. Then you have something real to compare against a retainer.
